text:
Also, you only gave me a summary of the algernative framings, not the title/summary/rationale/etc that k asked for
 [...] You're right that I over-compressed the essay angles — here's the full breakdown for all 8, exactly as generated:

---

## 1. "Oracle."
**Summary:** Correctness isn't proven once in a test suite — it's witnessed continuously, so Trellis ships its slow, obviously-correct twin into production and checks itself against it on every transaction.

**TL;DR:** Tests certify the past; an oracle certifies the present. Trellis runs a full-recompute reference implementation *in production*, not just CI, diffing the clever incremental engine against the dumb exhaustive one on live traffic. A reader walks away believing "tested" and "verified" are different words, and that distrusting your own optimization is a shippable feature.

**Rationale:** "Receipts" explains behavior after the fact; this isolates *checking* behavior while it happens — the relationship between a fast implementation and a slow specification. Only angle touching testing culture.

**Why pick this one:** Most technically surprising claim in the project — everyone runs oracles in tests, almost nobody pays for one in production. Generalizes furthest: anyone with a cache, index, or denormalized view can apply "keep the dumb version alive and let it vote" tomorrow.

**Outline:**
- A test is a memory; production is where you have amnesia
- The standard move (fuzz clever vs. dumb in CI, then discard the dumb one) — the discarding is the mistake
- Trellis keeps it: full recompute runs beside the incremental diff in production, disagreement is loud
- Objection: "that's twice the work" → it's the cost you already admitted was cheap (cost model), buys you a page instead of a heisenbug
- An optimization is a claim; claims want auditors
- Widen: caches, materialized views, denormalized counters are all unproven theorems running in production
- Close: trust is not a feeling, it's a diff that comes back empty

---

## 2. "Price Tag."
**Summary:** Trellis states O(total-state) per transaction on the front page because a confessed cost is a design constraint you can build around, while a hidden cost is a debt collected at the worst possible time.

**TL;DR:** Every abstraction has a bill; the only choice is itemized or surprise. Frameworks that hide their amortized cliffs are lying with benchmarks. An honest slow number beats a dishonest fast one.

**Rationale:** Only angle about economics and the rhetoric of performance claims — a cost model as part of a system's interface, as binding as its type signatures.

**Why pick this one:** Most defensible against self-promotion, since its center of mass is confessing a weakness. Earns credibility that transfers to every other Trellis essay.

**Outline:**
- Every README says fast; none says what it costs — "fast" is an ad, not a number
- Itemized cost (designed around) vs. collection notice (the amortized cliff hits in production)
- Trellis's confession: O(total-state), stated as a design consequence, not a footnote
- Complexity classes are contract terms; hiding one is fine print
- A stated cost lets the user decide the trade instead of discovering it was made for them
- Address the flinch: won't people bounce off the slow number? Yes — the ones for whom it's genuinely wrong. That's the number working
- Close: a benchmark is a performance; a cost model is a promise

---

## 3. "Shadow."
**Summary:** New infrastructure should earn deletion rights — run beside the old code, match it on live traffic, and only then, as the *last* step of adoption, does the bespoke code die.

**TL;DR:** The rewrite pitch always asks for faith first: delete, then find out. Shadow mode inverts the burden of proof. General discipline: never grant trust that hasn't been demonstrated on your own traffic.

**Rationale:** Only angle about migration and trust between systems — social/organizational, not architectural. Uniquely lets the essay argue *against* its own project's adoption.

**Why pick this one:** Broadest audience — everyone's survived a rewrite that asked for faith and delivered an incident. Has a real evidence-based ending (NMP's shadow-mode equivalence).

**Outline:**
- The familiar crime scene: the rewrite that started by deleting the old thing
- Name the inversion: new code is the defendant, not the judge
- Mechanics: shadow mode runs beside existing logic, diffs silently on real inputs
- One-paragraph bridge: effects-as-data is what makes the diff possible at all
- The NMP story, briefly
- Generalize: shadow the new database driver, the new pricing engine, anything
- Close: "deleting your bespoke code is the last step of adoption, not the first" — said about his own project, where it does the most work

---

## 4. "Absence."
**Summary:** The worst bugs are missing events, not wrong values — invisible because our entire debugging toolkit can only inspect what exists, never what should have happened.

**TL;DR:** You can't diff an effect performed three states ago, and definitely can't diff one that never happened. Leaks are bugs of omission, undetectable unless something knows the complete set of obligations. Omission bugs demand reconciliation, not vigilance.

**Rationale:** The epistemology essay — subject is the bug class itself, not any feature of the solution. Could be valued by someone who never adopts Trellis. The natural prequel/middle to "Structure" and "Receipts."

**Why pick this one:** Most natural successor in the site's own arc — trilogies want their second act. Strongest single image: the handle that outlived its reason.

**Outline:**
- The 3am scene inverted: nothing wrong in the state dump, but the relay connection count keeps climbing
- Taxonomy: bugs of commission (tools see these) vs. omission (tools are structurally blind)
- Anatomy of the leak: state → subscription → callback fired → handle saved → state gone → handle stays, nothing ties resource to reason
- Why every tool fails: you can't grep for a missing line
- The only real fix: something must hold the full set of obligations so absence becomes computable as a diff
- That's what a reconciler is, stripped of jargon: a machine for noticing absences
- Close: presence is cheap to check; absence requires a theory of what should exist

---

## 5. "1975."
**Summary:** An AI agent debugging a live system today works exactly like a 1975 programmer — read source, add a print, guess, reproduce — because we made source legible to machines and left runtime behavior just as illegible to them as to us.

**TL;DR:** Agents can read a million lines of source in a minute but are reduced to archaeology diagnosing production. Receipts turn diagnosis into lookup; dry runs mean an agent never has to gamble. Legibility-to-machines is the next systems requirement.

**Rationale:** Makes the non-human operator the protagonist for the full essay. Humans compensate for illegibility with intuition and tribal knowledge; an agent has neither — only text. The only forward-looking angle.

**Why pick this one:** Timeliest, widest reach — travels into the agents discourse, where the 2026 readership actually is. Reframes Trellis as an early instance of a coming requirement.

**Outline:**
- The anachronism played straight: describe the read/print/guess loop, then reveal it's a state-of-the-art agent today
- Why: we made source machine-legible; runtime behavior got nothing
- What humans use to cope (intuition, war stories) and why an agent has none of it — illegibility disqualifies rather than merely degrades
- What an agent actually needs: answers as data, consequences without commitment
- Trellis as existence proof, kept brief: flight recorder, rehearsable transactions
- The inversion: stop asking how to make agents smart enough for our systems — make systems answerable enough for agents
- Close: the 1975 programmer wasn't dumb; the machine was mute. Ours still is, and we're about to hire a billion operators who can't tolerate that

---

## 6. "Rehearsal."
**Summary:** Because effects are data and state is a cloneable graph, cloning gives you a free parallel universe — run any transaction, read exactly what it would do, discard the universe — turning "what would happen?" from a bet into a question.

**TL;DR:** Most systems support only one tense: the irreversible present. A dry run falls out for free once effects are values and state is cloneable. Counterfactuals become a first-class primitive most architectures accidentally forbid.

**Rationale:** "Receipts" faces backward (why did that happen?); this faces forward (what would happen?) — genuinely different capability, not retrofittable the way logging is. The only angle centered on pleasure/wonder rather than grievance.

**Why pick this one:** The strongest demonstration essay — can show an actual rehearsal rather than just argue, letting the capability sell itself.

**Outline:**
- The gamble everyone knows: hovering over Enter on a production command, having deduced the outcome
- Name the missing tense: systems speak only the irreversible present, no subjunctive
- Why it's usually impossible: effects are entangled with execution; mocks lie
- The unlock: clone + run + read + discard is a complete simulator, for free, as a consequence not a feature
- The walkthrough (center of mass): a concrete rehearsal against a tenex-edge-shaped state, showing the returned commands
- What changes when hypotheticals are cheap: operators rehearse, tests interrogate, agents never gamble
- Close: guessing is a tax the past charges, gambling a tax the future charges — Receipts settled the first, this settles the second

---

## 7. "When."
**Summary:** The callback asks "what should I do *when* X happens?" — wrong question for anything long-lived, because the answer outlives its reason; the right question is "what should exist, *given* the state?"

**TL;DR:** Event-driven culture trained us to program in "when," and "when" has no memory — the instant after a callback fires, cause and effect are severed. Every leaked handle is that severed connection.

**Rationale:** The polemic — the only angle targeting a dominant paradigm rather than a bug, cost, or capability. "Absence" diagnoses the wound; "When" indicts the weapon.

**Why pick this one:** Pick it for a fight worth having — attacking the observer pattern by name generates the strongest reaction of any of the eight. Needs the least Trellis-specific context; the project appears only as a consequence.

**Outline:**
- The whiteboard where every architecture is born: "when X, subscribe" — innocent sentences, each a leak in marker
- Dissect the grammar: "when X, do Y" executes Y and forgets X; effect persists, reason evaporates
- The observer pattern's rap sheet: a machine for creating orphans
- Steelman "when": fine for genuinely instantaneous things (logs, metrics); fails for anything with a lifetime
- The alternative grammar: "given this state, these things exist" — closing becomes a diff, not anyone's job
- Concede the cost: "given" requires recomputing the world; "when" is cheap the way unsecured credit is cheap
- Close: when is for logs, given is for everything you'll have to clean up

---

## 8. "Tuition."
**Summary:** Nostr clients — a standing negotiation with unreliable relays where every UI state change silently creates open/close obligations — are the perfect leak-generating machine, and they beat this architecture into him.

**TL;DR:** Some lessons can only be bought from a domain that punishes you, and nostr charges the highest tuition for effect-lifecycle mistakes. Trellis is the receipt for that tuition.

**Rationale:** The only first-person-narrative angle — argues from scar tissue, not principle. Isolates the relationship between domain and doctrine: why certain environments force certain architectures.

**Why pick this one:** Trust and differentiation — a specific, dated account of failure isn't a commodity the way abstract-architecture essays are. Makes every other Trellis essay read as testimony instead of pitch.

**Outline:**
- A specific war story: a user switches profiles, forty relay subscriptions from the old profile keep streaming
- Why nostr is the perfect adversary: no sessions, no single server, the protocol never tells you what you forgot to close
- The escalation ladder actually climbed: discipline → convention → tooling → despair — each rung the same lie, that vigilance scales
- The turn: the domain wasn't punishing the code, it was punishing the question (one-line link to "When")
- What tuition bought: full-state reconciliation, effects-as-data, the oracle — each traced to a specific scar
- The meta-claim, earned by now: architecture comes from a domain vicious enough to falsify your habits
- Close: Trellis is the diploma; the frame is every handle he ever forgot to close

---

The agent's own top-3 pick for what to write next: **Absence** (completes the arc), **1975** (widest audience), **Tuition** (buys credibility for everything after it).
